nameStory: The 'fly' in fly honeysuckle refers to this shrub's ability to attract flies and other small insects to its flowers for pollination. Unlike its sweet-smelling cousins, this honeysuckle doesn't rely on bees alone but welcomes a variety of flying visitors. The name distinguishes it from the more familiar vining honeysuckles that climb and twist.
description: Fly honeysuckle is a compact deciduous shrub that typically grows 3-6 feet tall with an upright, bushy form. This European native produces small, paired flowers in spring followed by glossy red berries that catch the eye in summer. Unlike the climbing honeysuckles many people know, this one stays put as a well-behaved shrub. Its oval leaves are arranged in opposite pairs along gray-brown stems.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Glossy red berries (occasionally yellow) appear in pairs, hanging from short stalks like tiny ornaments. The berries feel firm and smooth to the touch, and each contains about 4-5 seeds.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval leaves are arranged in opposite pairs along the stems, with a soft, slightly fuzzy texture on the undersides. They're medium green and have a simple, unlobed shape with smooth or slightly wavy edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, paired yellowish-white flowers appear in spring, sitting close to the stem rather than in showy clusters. Each flower has a tubular shape typical of honeysuckles but lacks the strong fragrance of other species.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a compact, upright shrub with multiple stems from the base, rarely exceeding 6 feet tall. The branching pattern is dense and bushy rather than sprawling or climbing.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are smooth and gray-brown, while older bark develops thin, papery strips that peel slightly. The bark has a pleasant, woody smell when scratched.

habitat: Fly honeysuckle is occasionally found in New England as an escape from cultivation, typically in disturbed areas, woodland edges, and old gardens. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate both sun and partial shade. You might spot it near abandoned homesites or in areas where European plants have naturalized.

seasonality.spring: Small paired flowers bloom in late spring, appearing as yellowish-white tubes nestled close to the stems. New leaves emerge bright green and soft.
seasonality.summer: The distinctive glossy red berries ripen and become the plant's most noticeable feature, persisting for about two weeks before birds discover them.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, and any remaining berries become more visible as the foliage thins.
seasonality.winter: The bare shrub shows its branching pattern clearly, with gray-brown stems and small buds that help identify it even without leaves.

funFact: The berries of fly honeysuckle contain almost 90% water and can cause stomach upset in children who eat about 30 or more - but birds love them and can safely gobble them up to spread the seeds around the neighborhood.
confusionNotes: The paired red berries make this easy to distinguish from most other honeysuckles, which typically have berries in clusters or different colors. Remember: 'fly honeysuckle, berries in twos' - the berries always appear as a pair rather than singly or in bunches.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'fly honeysuckle,' this shrub is not native to New England but rather a European species that was brought here as an ornamental plant. Don't confuse it with our native American fly honeysuckle, which has blue-black berries instead of red ones.
compareHints: Fly honeysuckle stands out from other honeysuckles in New England by its paired red berries and shrubby growth habit - most others either climb like vines or have different colored berries. American fly honeysuckle has blue-black berries, while invasive species like Morrow's honeysuckle have berries in clusters rather than pairs. The compact shrub form also distinguishes it from the aggressive, spreading invasive honeysuckles.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike the invasive Japanese, Morrow's, and Tatarian honeysuckles that dominate many New England areas, American fly-honeysuckle has distinctively paired berries and a much more restrained growth habit.
Japanese honeysuckle is unique among New England honeysuckles for its white-to-yellow color change and semi-evergreen leaves.
Unlike native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Morrow's honeysuckle has flowers and berries strictly in pairs with red fruit.
Unlike native American fly-honeysuckle which stays small and has paired flowers on long stalks, Amur honeysuckle grows into a large shrub with flowers sitting directly on the branches.
Among New England honeysuckles, coral honeysuckle is the only one with scentless, coral-red tubular flowers and that distinctive leaf-fusion around the stem.
Among New England's honeysuckles, glaucous honeysuckle is the only climbing species with that distinctive waxy blue-green leaf coating and cup-forming fused upper leaves.
Unlike our native fly honeysuckles which have flowers in clusters and blue or black berries, Tatarian honeysuckle always has paired flowers and red berries.
Mountain fly-honeysuckle differs from American fly honeysuckle by having much fuzzier leaves and preferring higher elevation habitats.
Among New England's honeysuckles, the dense coating of soft hairs immediately separates this species from smooth-leaved Japanese honeysuckle or the only slightly hairy American fly honeysuckle.
Unlike the vigorous vining Japanese honeysuckle, winter honeysuckle is a well-behaved shrub that doesn't climb.
Unlike the more common American fly honeysuckle which prefers drier woods, swamp fly honeysuckle demands wet feet and boggy conditions.

Unlike the ubiquitous Japanese honeysuckle which blooms white to yellow and has simple opposite leaves, common honeysuckle has those distinctive fused upper leaves and more intensely fragrant flowers.
While New England has many honeysuckle species, perfoliate honeysuckle is the only one with fused upper leaves that the stem appears to grow through.
Unlike the invasive Asian honeysuckles that plague New England (Japanese, Morrow's, Amur), twinberry honeysuckle doesn't spread aggressively and has the unique twin-berry-in-red-bracts feature.
Unlike the aggressive Japanese honeysuckle that stays white then turns yellow, grape honeysuckle flowers age to pink.
Unlike its weedy relatives like Japanese honeysuckle (which climbs) or Morrow's honeysuckle (which has red berries), sweetberry honeysuckle stays compact and produces edible blue fruit.
